---
# On Mending

My grandmother kept a wooden box beside her sewing chair, and inside it lived a jumble of things that had outlived their purpose and not yet been thrown away: spools with a few inches of thread left, a tin of mismatched buttons, a pair of scissors with one handle wrapped in electrical tape, a thimble worn thin on one side. When a sock developed a hole at the heel, she didn't throw it out. She stretched it over a wooden egg, found the nearest thread that roughly matched, and wove small, careful lines across the gap until the hole became a patch, and the patch became a kind of signature. I remember being fascinated by those darns as a child. They were uglier than the original fabric and somehow more beautiful, because you could see that someone had cared enough to stay with the problem.

I have been thinking about that box lately, and about mending in general, because it seems to me that repair is one of the most underrated forms of attention we have. We live in a culture that prefers replacement. Phones are sealed with glue, batteries are fused into casings, and a broken appliance often costs more to fix than to replace with a newer model that will be just as difficult to open when it fails. The economics are well known. What is less discussed is what this does to us as people. If every failure is an occasion to discard, we slowly lose the habit of looking closely at things, of asking how they work, of wondering what holds them together.

Mending demands that you understand an object's structure. You have to find where the stress falls, where the seam was weakest, which part was never meant to bear weight. A broken chair leg tells you something about how the chair was built and how it was used. A torn coat tells you about the places where you have been moving through the world. Repair is a conversation with the thing itself, and it is slower and more humble than buying something new, because it requires you to admit that you do not already know everything about it.

---

There is a Japanese art form called kintsugi, in which broken ceramics are repaired with lacquer mixed with powdered gold. The cracks are not hidden. They are highlighted, so that the broken bowl becomes a map of its own history, glowing where it once fractured. I first encountered this idea in a museum years ago, standing in front of a tea bowl whose seams ran like rivers of light across its dark glaze. I remember thinking it was a lovely metaphor for grief or for recovery, and it is. But I have come to think the deeper lesson is about honesty. Kintsugi refuses to pretend the break never happened. It treats the damage as part of the object's story rather than an embarrassment to be erased.

We are not usually so generous with ourselves. When something in our lives breaks, whether a friendship, a habit, a body, or a sense of direction, we tend to want the old version back as quickly as possible, or else we want to discard the whole thing and begin again somewhere else. Both impulses are understandable. But there is another option, which is to stay with the break long enough to learn its shape, and then to repair it in a way that acknowledges what happened. The repaired thing is not the same as the original. It may be less smooth, but it carries information that the unbroken version could never hold.

---

Of course, not every repair is worth making. Some things are beyond saving, and an honest mender knows when to let go. My grandmother once spent an entire afternoon trying to rescue a wool blanket that had been eaten through by moths in a dozen places. She eventually gave up and cut it into squares for a quilt, which I still have. I used to think of that as a defeat, but she didn't see it that way. The blanket had become something else, and she was content to let it. Repair is not the same as nostalgia. Sometimes the most respectful thing you can do for an object is to transform it rather than restore it.

This is a distinction worth holding onto, because the cultural conversation about sustainability can make repair sound like a moral duty in every case. It is not. A person with a demanding job and three children and a leaking roof does not owe the world an hour of hand-stitching for every pair of trousers. Mending is a practice, not a penance, and it works best when it is pursued for its own sake, because it feels good to make something hold together. The satisfaction is real: the small click of a repaired hinge, the first time a zipper runs smoothly again, the quiet pride of a seam that will outlast its predecessor.

---

I want to say something about time, because repair is fundamentally about time. A repaired object has a longer life than it otherwise would have, and in that extension there is a kind of resistance to the idea that everything is disposable. When you mend a thing, you agree to keep it company for a while longer. You become, however briefly, its steward. I think this is part of why people feel tender toward heirlooms and old tools, even when the objects are not especially valuable. A hand plane that belonged to someone's father carries the marks of his hands. The wear on its wooden handle is a record of years of use, and using it again means taking up a share of that history.

There is an old idea that the ancient Greeks had a word, *ergon*, that meant both work and the function of a thing, the purpose for which it was made. A knife's ergon is to cut; a horse's is to run; a person's, in some philosophical traditions, is to live well. To repair something is to restore its ergon, to return it to the work it was meant to do. This is a surprisingly dignified way to think about a broken kettle or a torn bag. You are not merely fixing a problem. You are helping the object become again what it was for.

I find this idea oddly moving. It suggests that things have a kind of integrity, a shape they are trying to hold, and that our job as caretakers is to help them keep that shape. It also suggests that we have a shape of our own, which we lose when we are broken and must patiently recover. Perhaps that is why mending feels so good. It is a rehearsal for a kind of self-repair, a practice in patience and in the willingness to be useful to something that cannot thank you.

---

When I was younger, I thought of competence as the ability to do difficult things quickly. Now I think competence is closer to the ability to stay calm in the presence of something broken. The person who can sit down with a damaged object, examine it without panic, and say, "Let's see how this works," has a kind of maturity that cannot be taught in a weekend workshop. It comes from years of small failures and small recoveries, from the experience of discovering that most things can be understood if you are willing to look long enough.

This patience is increasingly rare, and I suspect we are poorer for losing it. The modern world offers us endless novelty, and novelty is seductive because it asks nothing of us. A new object arrives complete, with no history and no flaws, and we are invited to enjoy it without understanding it. Repair asks the opposite. It asks us to participate, to get our hands dirty, to accept that the thing in front of us has its own logic and its own resistance. In return, it gives us a relationship with the world that is deeper than consumption.

---

I do not want to romanticize the past too much. My grandmother's darning was born partly of necessity; her generation did not have the luxury of disposable socks, and the box beside her chair existed because scarcity demanded it. There was nothing noble about being poor, and I would not want to return to the conditions that made thrift a daily discipline. But the skills she carried, the habit of looking closely and fixing what could be fixed, are not inherently tied to hardship. They are simply forms of care, and care is available to anyone.

What would it mean to bring that care back into ordinary life? It might mean learning to sew a button, or to replace a bicycle chain, or to solder a loose wire. It might mean asking, before buying something new, whether the old thing could be made to work again. It might also mean extending the same patience to people, to relationships, and to ourselves. We are all, in some sense, objects that have been used and worn and occasionally broken. We deserve the same attention a good mender gives to a cracked bowl or a frayed collar: a willingness to find the weak point, to understand the stress, and to repair without pretending the damage never happened.

---

The wooden egg my grandmother used for darning is still in my possession. It is smooth from years of handling, and one end has a small chip where it once struck the edge of a table. I keep it on a shelf near my desk. Sometimes, when I am tempted to throw away something that has stopped working, I pick up the egg and turn it over in my hand, and I think about the afternoons she spent weaving thread across holes that no one else would have noticed. The thought usually stops me. I go find a screwdriver, or a needle, or a little glue, and I sit down to see how the thing was made.

It is not always successful. Some repairs fail, and some objects remain broken. But the attempt itself changes the way I see the world. It reminds me that most of what surrounds me was made by someone, held together by decisions I can partly understand, and capable of being cared for if I am willing to slow down. In a culture that rewards speed and replacement, that is a small but real act of resistance, and it is one my grandmother taught me without ever calling it that.

She would have laughed at the idea that a sock darn could be philosophy. To her, it was simply what you did when something you cared about had a hole in it. Perhaps that is the best way to think about mending: not as a grand project of sustainability or self-improvement, but as the ordinary, humble act of refusing to abandon something just because it has become imperfect. Most of us, if we are honest, would like the same consideration for ourselves.
---

The piece is interested in patience, attention, and the difference between caring for something and insisting it return to its former state. Its invitation to the reader is practical as well as emotional: look closely, try to understand what is broken, and offer care without making repair an obligation or pretending damage did not happen.

The grandmother’s sewing box, the kintsugi bowl, the repurposed blanket, and the wooden egg give that theme a repeated material presence. Medium: the recurring wooden egg and the essay’s consistent, qualified emphasis on patient care make the chosen sensibility distinct within the sample, though it is expressed through a polished, familiar reflective-essay form.
